paragraphs: When evaluation problems have leaked into training, a language model’s apparent reasoning can reflect contamination rather than generalization. This paper studies what changes inside contaminated models. It identifies a signal involving mutual information between internal representations and gradients: the statistical connection between what the model represents and how its training objective responds becomes weaker.

The proposed explanation is geometric. Contaminated models concentrate their representations into fewer dominant directions, producing a lower-dimensional computation regime. On leaked inputs, this concentration weakens the linear relationship between representations and gradients. The authors analyze this relationship in a whitened space and show mathematically how the resulting narrowing implies reduced mutual information.

The paper also uses this analysis to restore reasoning behavior in contaminated models. It reports up to an 11.03% absolute improvement in average consistency with the base model over the strongest baseline. That result connects the geometric diagnosis to a practical intervention, with success measured by restored agreement with the base model’s behavior.
icml-2026-a-narrowing-geometry-in-contam.tldr: The paper links contaminated reasoning to increasingly concentrated internal representations and uses that analysis to help restore base-model reasoning behavior.

paragraphs: Neural networks that respect three-dimensional geometric transformations use tensor products to let different feature types interact. These operations can be expensive. The paper addresses a distinction in accelerating them: some earlier speedups reduce the interactions the network can express, while an algorithmic improvement should compute the complete operation more efficiently.

The authors develop a complete algorithm for Clebsch–Gordan tensor products, reducing the stated runtime complexity from O(L^6) to O(L^4 log² L), close to the O(L^4) lower bound. Their derivation connects Fourier-based convolution to Gaunt tensor products, then addresses the interactions missing from that construction because of antisymmetry issues.

The solution extends scalar signals to signals carrying richer transformation structure, using tensor spherical harmonics and a generalized Gaunt formula. The authors prove that vector-valued signals are sufficient to recover the missing interactions. The contribution is therefore a theoretical acceleration that retains the full tensor product, preserving the feature interactions that less complete shortcuts can omit.
icml-2026-asymptotically-fast-clebsch-go.tldr: A complete Clebsch–Gordan tensor-product algorithm uses vector spherical harmonics to reduce asymptotic computation without dropping interactions.

paragraphs: Graphs with text attached to their nodes require models to combine language meaning with connection structure. Existing chain-of-thought approaches can keep these parts too separate: reasoning proceeds while the graph representation remains fixed. This paper proposes KCoT, a framework in which reasoning and graph representation learning develop together.

Its theoretical foundation is a formal correspondence between a Transformer block and the assignment-and-update operations of k-means clustering. This provides an interpretation of iterative reasoning as repeatedly organizing information and refining its representation. KCoT turns that interpretation into a Semantic Discriminating Prompt that explicitly structures the reasoning around those operations.

A structure-grounded alignment strategy then combines graph topology with representations that change as reasoning progresses. This matters because the model can bring semantic and structural information together at successive steps, rather than relying on one fixed graph encoding. Experiments on standard benchmarks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the usefulness of this clustering-based design for the evaluated graph-learning tasks.
icml-2026-clustering-as-reasoning-a-k-me.tldr: KCoT connects Transformer computation to k-means clustering to jointly develop step-by-step reasoning and graph representations.

paragraphs: Stable training depends on controlling how model computations change as parameters are updated. Maximal Update Parametrization, or μP, provides a theoretical basis for keeping activation scale controlled across model widths. This paper argues that optimizers such as Muon only partly match that framework because they constrain updates while allowing the weights themselves to drift.

The proposed Spectral Sphere Optimizer constrains both weights and their updates at the level of individual modules. The authors derive a steepest-descent direction on this constrained space, producing an optimization process they describe as fully aligned with μP. They also implement the method as a parallel algorithm within Megatron to support large-scale training.

Pretraining experiments cover a dense 1.7-billion-parameter model, an 8-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 1 billion active parameters, and 200-layer DeepNet models. SSO consistently outperforms AdamW and Muon in these evaluations. Reported stability benefits include better expert-router load balancing, fewer outliers, and strictly bounded activations, connecting the mathematical constraints to observed training behavior.
icml-2026-controlled-llm-training-on-spe.tldr: SSO constrains both model weights and updates to improve optimization performance and stability in large-model pretraining.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses which expensive experiment or model configuration to evaluate next. It also needs a stopping decision: another evaluation may improve the answer, but incur more cost than the improvement justifies. This paper studies that trade-off through cost-adjusted simple regret, a measure that combines solution quality with accumulated evaluation cost.

The authors propose a stopping rule that adapts to changing evaluation costs without heuristic tuning. Its justification comes from a theoretical connection to two cost-aware acquisition functions, PBGI and LogEIPC. When the stopping rule is paired with either of these functions, they prove a bound on expected cost-adjusted simple regret.

Experiments include synthetic problems, hyperparameter optimization, and neural architecture size search. The proposed pairings usually match or outperform other combinations of acquisition functions and stopping rules on the cost-adjusted measure. The qualification matters: the empirical result is generally favorable, while the theoretical guarantee applies to the specified pairings. Together, these results make stopping part of the optimization objective itself.
icml-2026-cost-aware-stopping-for-bayesi.tldr: A theoretically grounded stopping rule helps Bayesian optimization balance further solution improvements against evaluation costs.

paragraphs: Building a 3D scene from a monocular video with few viewpoints creates a tension between covering the scene and keeping its representation compact. Hierarchical training with interpolated frames improves coverage, but repeated merging and correlated artificial viewpoints introduce structured duplication. According to the paper, this redundancy undermines the independence assumptions behind standard pruning and makes global thresholds ineffective.

CoverPruneGS removes redundant Gaussian primitives through a coarse-to-fine process. It first selects locally diverse primitives within voxels. It then refines those choices using randomized dropout rendering and comparisons against ground-truth images, allowing the method to assess which removals damage the reconstruction.

A CUDA attribution mechanism accounts for each Gaussian’s image footprint and aggregates error increases over affected pixels. These importance scores support quantile-based rescue of essential primitives, helping preserve coverage during compression. Across multiple datasets, the method reports a 56.8% reduction in Gaussian count and faster inference while maintaining or improving novel-view synthesis quality. The results connect compactness to preserving useful scene coverage.
icml-2026-coverprunegs-coverage-preservi.tldr: CoverPruneGS removes structured redundancy from 3D Gaussian scenes while rescuing primitives needed to preserve reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: Adversarial inputs developed against one vision-language model often transfer poorly to another. This paper attributes that difficulty to differences in models’ safety alignment: an attack may exploit peculiarities of its development model instead of features shared across models. Using linear probes, the authors identify safety-related representations concentrated in particular intermediate neural circuits.

The proposed Safety Circuit Intervention Attack uses this internal distinction to steer representations. Its two objectives reduce the influence of localized safety-related circuitry while strengthening representations described as more transferable across models. The framework also includes contrastive semantic steering and spectral smoothness regularization, intended to shape the semantic direction of the intervention and keep the resulting visual perturbations coherent.

Experiments report that SCIA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art attacks on unseen black-box vision-language models. The finding supports the paper’s account that separating model-specific safety behavior from shared features can improve attack transfer in the tested setting. Its research significance lies in connecting an internal representation analysis with observed weaknesses in the transfer robustness of safety mechanisms.
icml-2026-dissecting-the-safety-circuit-.tldr: SCIA links localized safety representations to attack transferability and reports stronger attacks against unseen vision-language models.

paragraphs: A proof sketch divides a difficult theorem into a high-level strategy and smaller subgoals that can be proved independently. Language models can generate these sketches, but a rigid sketch makes correction expensive. Revising one part may require rebuilding the whole structure and discarding work on subgoals that have already been proved.

EditableSketch makes the proof plan revisable in place. It supports correcting errors and breaking a subgoal into smaller pieces while retaining previously proved subgoals. The accompanying SketchRefine framework repeatedly improves a proof through these localized edits. The approach makes preservation of completed work an explicit part of the proof-generation process.

Experiments report both reduced proof costs and stronger performance. On FormalMath-Lite, the method reaches a 76.0% pass rate, with a reported 14.1% improvement over DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B. Against Hilbert, it achieves comparable performance with substantially lower token overhead. These findings suggest that revisable proof structure can improve the efficiency of automated theorem proving while also helping the system complete more proofs.
icml-2026-editable-proof-sketch-for-auto.tldr: EditableSketch lets theorem-proving systems revise proof plans locally while preserving completed subgoals, reducing cost and improving reported performance.

paragraphs: Enlarging real-world images by four times or more requires recovering detail from inputs affected by complex degradation. HYPIR performs well on many images, but its single forward step leaves fine detail unresolved in some challenging cases. Simply cascading two stages improves appearance while introducing oversaturation, weak textures, and higher latency.

HYPIR++ changes both restoration and training. It removes the degradation-removal encoder and noise augmentation modules to retain fidelity cues from the low-quality input. An optimized latent ConvNeXt and a latent patch discriminator enable adversarial learning within the latent representation, targeting clearer detail and more stable local structure.

The method also shortens text sequences and replaces full attention with sparse attention over neighbors. These changes support efficient high-resolution inference without splitting the image into tiles. Experiments report improved perceptual quality and a 1.71-times speedup over HYPIR on large-factor real-world super-resolution. The contribution combines changes to detail reconstruction with computational changes, addressing the quality and latency problems together.
icml-2026-enhanced-latent-space-adversar.tldr: HYPIR++ combines latent-space adversarial learning with more efficient attention to improve super-resolution quality and run 1.71 times faster than HYPIR.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning adapts language models using data held across decentralized devices. Those devices can have very different computing and communication resources. Existing truncation-based approaches often tie the amount of model information a device receives to the amount it can train. This wastes available bandwidth on devices that communicate well but have limited computing capacity, and can distort local gradients.

FedHera separates receiving information from optimizing parameters. Its allocation strategy preserves spectral information and transfers as much global knowledge as bandwidth allows, independently of the device’s training constraints. A client can therefore receive a richer representation than the portion it can afford to update.

A prefix-gating mechanism uses that downloaded, higher-capacity basis as a frozen reference for local learning. This reference guides updates and reduces the optimization gap introduced by aggressive truncation. Experiments across different resource-heterogeneity settings report improved stability and accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support treating communication capacity and trainable capacity as separate design choices.
icml-2026-fedhera-towards-drift-resilien.tldr: FedHera separates downloaded model capacity from locally trainable capacity to improve federated fine-tuning under unequal device resources.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can describe content that is absent from an image when it gives too little attention to relevant visual evidence or loses that evidence as generation continues. This paper finds that sensitivity to the correct evidence varies across layers. Even when overall visual attention is weak, particular layers can still identify useful image information.

ILVAD uses this discrepancy to construct a saliency map. It examines attention from early generated tokens to visual tokens across layers, identifying visual tokens that are repeatedly activated. The map then increases attention to that evidence during subsequent generation, aiming to reduce the model’s tendency to forget what it saw.

The same map also measures how strongly generated text attends to visual evidence, allowing the method to select and emphasize grounded text tokens. ILVAD requires no training and is designed as a plug-in intervention. Evaluations on multiple benchmarks and five models report consistent hallucination mitigation across architectures, supporting the usefulness of preserving visual evidence throughout generation.
icml-2026-finding-the-correct-visual-evi.tldr: ILVAD uses differences in attention across layers to identify visual evidence and keep generated responses grounded in it without additional training.

paragraphs: Coding agents handle tasks such as exploring repositories, testing software, and designing architecture, while prominent benchmarks emphasize individual issue fixes. This paper asks how training can develop abilities that transfer across these different activities. The authors break agent trajectories into fine-grained components to identify shared skills and derive principles for designing auxiliary training tasks.

Hybrid-Gym implements those principles through scalable synthetic tasks, including locating functions and searching dependencies. These tasks provide practice in components of broader coding work. The training environment is intended to teach reusable abilities that can support real-world tasks even when those downstream tasks are absent from training.

Experiments report gains over a base model of 25.4 percentage points on SWE-Bench Verified, 7.9% on SWT-Bench Verified, and 5.1% on Commit-0 Lite. Hybrid-Gym also complements downstream-task datasets, including a reported 4.9% improvement for SWE-Play on SWT-Bench Verified. These results support synthetic skill training as a useful contributor to coding-agent generalization across the evaluated tasks.
icml-2026-hybrid-gym-training-coding-age.tldr: Hybrid-Gym trains reusable coding skills through synthetic tasks and reports improvements on several real-world coding benchmarks.

paragraphs: Most deep learning models pass information through activation values. Biological information processing also involves changing phases and synchronization, which have been hypothesized to help coordinate related features. This paper draws on that idea by adding an evolving phase state to Vision Transformers through Kuramoto oscillatory Phase Encoding, or KoPE.

The added state introduces a synchronization mechanism alongside the model’s existing representations. The authors show that this can improve training, parameter, and data efficiency through better structure learning. The approach therefore explores synchronization as a computational mechanism for organizing information within a vision model, rather than only as a biological analogy.

Reported benefits extend to semantic and panoptic segmentation, alignment between visual and language representations, and few-shot abstract visual reasoning on ARC-AGI. Theoretical analysis and empirical checks further suggest that KoPE can accelerate attention concentration, offering an explanation for its efficiency benefits. Taken together, the findings indicate that evolving phase information can be useful across several tasks requiring structured visual understanding.
icml-2026-kuramoto-oscillatory-phase-enc.tldr: KoPE adds evolving, synchronizing phase states to Vision Transformers to improve learning efficiency and structured visual understanding.

paragraphs: Writing a scientific introduction requires more than fluent prose: its argument and citations should be faithful to the research. This paper defines Content-Conditional Introduction Generation, a task in which the introduction must be grounded in the paper’s core evidence. The formulation makes the underlying scientific logic an explicit part of the writing problem.

LECTOR first extracts a logic-reasoning graph from the paper’s main body. This graph serves as a verifiable plan for the introduction’s argument. A joint reward mechanism then optimizes both the graph’s structural fidelity and the quality of the resulting narrative, connecting reasoning structure with written expression.

The authors evaluate the framework on a dataset built from Nature Communications papers. They report consistent improvements in logic fidelity and introduction quality, including 26.7% in Graph Quality, 8.6% in Citation Quality, and 3.3% in Paper Consistency. These results support explicitly optimizing the relationship between a paper’s evidence, its argument structure, and its introduction, rather than evaluating prose quality alone.
icml-2026-lector-joint-optimization-of-s.tldr: LECTOR jointly improves an evidence-grounded reasoning graph and its written introduction to strengthen scientific logic, citations, and consistency.

paragraphs: Video language models sometimes produce plausible descriptions that the video does not support, especially when objects are difficult to see or interpret. Contrastive decoding tries to reduce these errors using altered inputs, but random alterations may miss the particular visual cues behind a model’s hallucinations. MACD makes construction of those comparison inputs specific to the model.

The method uses the video model’s own feedback to identify object regions most responsible for hallucination. It creates targeted object-level counterfactual inputs and incorporates them into contrastive decoding. The resulting comparison guides token selection toward visual evidence, connecting the intervention to the model’s observed weaknesses.

Evaluations on EventHallusion, MVBench, Perception-test, and Video-MME report consistent hallucination reductions while preserving or improving task accuracy. The findings span multiple video models, including Qwen and InternVL, with especially strong gains for small, occluded, or co-occurring objects. These results support targeted counterfactual construction as a useful inference-time approach to grounding video descriptions and answers.
icml-2026-macd-model-aware-contrastive-d.tldr: MACD uses model feedback to construct targeted visual counterfactuals that reduce video-model hallucinations during decoding.

paragraphs: Dynamic sparse training changes which model parameters are active during learning, offering a way to improve training and inference efficiency. In language-model training, however, changing that active structure can cause sudden loss spikes. This paper traces a source of instability to newly regrown parameters when standard Adam-based optimizers are used naively.

Those parameters experience a cold start in the optimizer, producing excessively large updates that disrupt training. Sparse Memory-Efficient Training, or SMET, introduces optimizer warm-up to stabilize this transition. It also scales the learning rate according to parameter density to improve training progress as the sparse configuration changes.

SMET saves memory by storing gradients and optimizer states only for active parameters. The authors provide a theoretical analysis of its update behavior showing improved optimization stability, alongside experiments demonstrating stable and scalable sparse language-model pretraining. The contribution addresses both the memory footprint of sparsity and the training dynamics needed to make that saving usable, supporting sparse training as a practical alternative to dense training.
icml-2026-memory-efficient-llm-training-.tldr: SMET stabilizes newly activated parameters in dynamic sparse training while reducing memory use through sparse gradient and optimizer-state storage.

paragraphs: Agents learning a sequence of cooperative tasks can benefit from reusing coordination skills found in recorded multi-agent behavior. A fixed skill library can become restrictive as tasks change and the skill space expands. The paper targets the resulting interference, forgetting of earlier abilities, and reduced capacity to learn new ones.

COMAD uses an autoencoder to extract reusable coordination skills from mixed offline behavior data. It then incorporates those skills into policy learning through a multi-head architecture. A density-based estimator assesses which skills are reusable and uses them to guide the advantage function, connecting skill discovery with the learning objective.

The skill library can expand continually, helping the system accommodate new coordination patterns while retaining useful existing ones. Theoretical analysis shows that the method approximates the optimum of a continual skill-discovery problem. Across diverse multi-agent reinforcement-learning benchmarks, COMAD reports better forward and backward transfer than multiple baselines. These results indicate benefits both for learning later tasks and for performance on previously encountered tasks.
icml-2026-offline-multi-agent-continual-.tldr: COMAD continually discovers, expands, and reuses coordination skills from offline data to improve transfer across sequential multi-agent tasks.

paragraphs: Traditional code-complexity measures were developed to assess properties such as software maintainability. This paper examines whether they also describe how difficult code is for language models. Its experiments find no consistent correlation between classical complexity metrics and model performance, suggesting that these measures miss aspects of difficulty relevant to LLMs.

The proposed LM-CC metric starts from the hypothesis that model-perceived difficulty is driven by semantic nonlinearity. It represents code through an entropy-guided hierarchy of semantic composition and measures the uncertainty accumulated during understanding. This shifts the focus toward how meaning is assembled and how uncertain that process is for a model.

The authors report strong, consistent partial correlations between LM-CC and LLM performance. They also find that reducing LM-CC while preserving program semantics consistently improves downstream task performance in their experiments. The two findings give complementary support: the metric tracks observed difficulty, and changes that lower it can make code easier for models to use without changing what the code does.
icml-2026-rethinking-code-complexity-thr.tldr: LM-CC measures code complexity through semantic uncertainty and correlates more consistently with language-model performance than classical metrics in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision models provide useful starting points, but deployment may require networks with different depths and widths. A fixed-size pretrained model does not directly solve that range of initialization needs. SWEET addresses the problem by learning a reusable weight template through self-supervised, constraint-based pretraining.

The framework uses Tucker-based factorization to separate a shared template from size-specific weight scalers. A target model is initialized by composing and reweighting the template using lightweight scalers, whose parameters can be learned from minimal training data. This makes architectural size variation part of the pretraining design rather than a separate initialization problem for every target.

To improve width expansion, SWEET introduces stochastic scaling along width-related dimensions. This regularizes the template and encourages representations that generalize across widths. Experiments on classification, detection, segmentation, and generation report state-of-the-art performance for initializing variable-sized vision models. The findings support reusable weight structure as a way to carry pretraining benefits across architectures with different capacity requirements.
icml-2026-self-supervised-weight-templat.tldr: SWEET learns a shared weight template and lightweight size-specific scalers to initialize vision models across different depths and widths.

paragraphs: Segment Anything Models can struggle on specialized segmentation tasks. Fine-tuning with task labels may help specialization but also cause overfitting, bias, and loss of generalization. SHERPA addresses this tension by using a smaller, task-adapted SAM to guide the fine-tuning of a larger model through features relevant to the target task.

Its Fisher Ratio Separation module separates highly task-relevant features, with the aim of preserving the larger model’s ability to handle other general tasks. A Guiding Feature Extraction module then obtains representative features from the fine-tuned smaller model. These features provide targeted guidance for adapting the larger SAM.

The authors use small models specialized for natural-image segmentation, biomedical-image segmentation, and video-object segmentation to guide larger SAM-series models. Experiments report improvements of up to 11.1% in retention of generalization ability and up to 2.2% in specific-task performance. These are reported upper gains across the evaluations, supporting the use of task-relevant guidance to improve specialization while better retaining broader segmentation abilities.
icml-2026-sherpa-fine-tuning-segment-any.tldr: SHERPA uses features from a smaller specialized SAM to improve a larger SAM’s task performance while better retaining generalization.

paragraphs: Adapting a generative model to a new distribution can require estimating the difference between two score functions. That difference also appears in diffusion post-training methods such as discriminator guidance. This paper addresses the difficulty of estimating it reliably while retaining scalability to high-dimensional settings.

The proposed estimator uses Sobolev regularization, which the authors identify as important both for statistical consistency and for stable learning with small samples. Their analysis establishes a convergence rate depending on sample size, dimension, and the smoothness of the underlying densities. It also provides a minimax lower bound in mean-squared error, describing a fundamental statistical constraint on this estimation problem.

Empirically, the regularized estimator is substantially more stable than existing methods in small-sample settings. The paper demonstrates its use in transfer learning for ECG signal generation, where it substantially outperforms non-regularized score-difference estimators on downstream classification. This connects the estimator’s mathematical properties with practical benefits when adapting a generative model from limited target data.
icml-2026-sobolev-regularized-score-diff.tldr: Sobolev regularization enables a consistent, scalable score-difference estimator with improved small-sample stability and demonstrated benefits for ECG generation transfer.

paragraphs: Training a team of language models creates a moving target: updating one agent changes the shared contexts encountered by its teammates. Sequential updates can therefore damage coordination even while modifying an individual component. TeamTR addresses this shift in the distribution of team interactions during fine-tuning.

The framework evaluates an agent update using rollouts from the intermediate team formed by updates already applied. It limits each agent’s behavioral change through a trust region measured with token-decomposed reverse KL. The authors derive population-level improvement lower bounds for individual updates and training stages, with a functional form that applies to any realized update order.

Those bounds motivate a practical certificate proxy based on logged surrogate objectives and KL terms. The implementation uses router-based text handoffs, sequence-level returns, and bounded group-normalized advantages. Experiments report fewer coordination regressions and more stable training across heterogeneous teams. A trust-region alignment step also supports replacing individual components, connecting controlled behavioral change to both joint training and modular team maintenance.
icml-2026-teamtr-trust-region-fine-tunin.tldr: TeamTR constrains agent updates using intermediate-team rollouts to reduce coordination regressions during multi-agent language-model fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Understanding a long video requires connecting events across time and deciding which moments matter for a question. Video-MTR treats this as an iterative decision process. The agent repeatedly chooses key video segments using both the query and the evolving context of frames it has already processed.

Training uses reinforcement-learning post-training with a gated reward system operating at two levels. A trajectory-level reward evaluates answer correctness, while turn-level rewards evaluate frame relevance to the query. Their combination is designed to support useful intermediate reasoning and training stability without requiring a data-intensive supervised fine-tuning stage.

The paper reports competitive or superior performance using about 8,000 training samples, compared with approaches requiring 257,000 to 4.4 million examples. Evaluations include VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench, LVBench, and EgoSchema, with reported improvements over state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and efficiency. The findings support learning where to look over multiple turns as an effective, data-efficient component of long-video understanding in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-video-mtr-reinforced-multi-tur.tldr: Video-MTR uses reinforcement learning to select relevant video segments over multiple turns, achieving strong long-video results with about 8,000 training samples.

paragraphs: Reward models learn to prefer chosen responses over rejected ones, commonly using the Bradley–Terry loss. This paper shows that the size of a pair’s learning update depends on more than prediction error. It also depends on the distance between the pair’s representations in the final layer’s output space.

That extra dependence can distort training. A misranked pair with nearby representations may receive a very weak update, while a distant pair receives a disproportionately strong one. Large-distance pairs can consequently dominate learning, even though distinguishing nearby responses is especially important for fine-grained judgments.

NormBT introduces adaptive normalization for each response pair to balance these distance-driven effects and focus learning more directly on prediction error. It is a lightweight modification to the existing loss with negligible overhead. Across several language-model backbones and datasets, the authors report consistent reward-model improvements, including gains exceeding 5% on RewardBench’s Reasoning category. That category contains many fine-grained pairs, aligning the observed benefit with the mechanism the paper identifies.
icml-2026-when-distance-distracts-repres.tldr: NormBT normalizes preference-learning updates to reduce representation-distance bias and improve reward models’ handling of fine-grained response differences.

paragraphs: Removing a concept from a text-to-video diffusion model depends on where that concept is represented. This paper finds that semantic information is distributed unevenly across model depth. At some layers, the target concept is more separable from other information; elsewhere, target and non-target signals remain strongly entangled.

The authors call this relationship concept–layer topological alignment. It explains a structural difficulty for depth-specific erasure: editing a layer where the relevant signals are entangled limits the effectiveness of the intervention. The proposed CLEAR framework therefore treats identifying suitable representational depths as part of the concept-erasure problem itself.

CLEAR formulates layer selection as an optimization over target-versus-non-target separability. Its objective favors layers where this separation is stronger, explicitly enforcing the alignment principle. Experiments on large-scale text-to-video diffusion models report more precise concept suppression while preserving overall generative quality. The findings support choosing intervention locations according to the model’s existing representation structure, so that suppression can be more selective.
icml-2026-where-concept-erasure-should-o.tldr: CLEAR selects layers where target concepts are more separable from other content to improve concept erasure while preserving video-generation quality.
